title: How to Find Customer Issues Across Surveys, Reviews and Call Center Transcripts
summary: Code every channel against one theme set, compare shares within each channel, and rank issues by impact and contact cost. A five-step how-to.
body_markdown:
Most enterprises already collect what they need to see their customers' problems. The survey team reads net promoter score (NPS) comments, the digital team watches app and Trustpilot reviews, and the contact center has thousands of call transcripts a week. The trouble is that each channel gets read on its own, with its own categories, so nobody can say whether the delivery complaint in the survey is the same problem driving calls. Customers don't stay in one channel either.[Gartner found](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11-13-customer-service-and-support-leaders-must-dismantle-service-doom-loops0) that 30% of customers end up using three or more channels.


To find customer issues across surveys, reviews and call center transcripts, code every channel against one shared set of themes, compare each theme's share within each channel rather than raw counts, and rank issues by their impact on your score and the contacts they generate, not by how often they're mentioned. Thematic does this with[lenses](https://getthematic.com/insights/lenses-context-layer-customer-intelligence) , which combine several datasets and analyze them together with a single, unified set of themes, so one issue carries one name and one count in every channel.


Below are the five steps, a worked example from a UK bank, and the mistakes that make cross-channel analysis mislead.


## The five-step process


1. **Bring each channel in with the fields you'll need:** date, channel, a customer or account ID, and any score.
2. **Prepare call transcripts before you analyze them:** keep the customer's words and separate why they called from what caused it.
3. **Code every channel against one theme set,** not one taxonomy per tool.
4. **Compare each theme's share within each channel,** because every channel has a built-in bias.
5. **Rank issues by impact and cost,** then trace the top ones back to the comments.


## Step 1: Bring each channel in with the fields you'll need


Each source needs four fields beyond the text: a date, the channel it came from, a customer or account identifier, and any score attached to it (NPS, customer satisfaction or CSAT, star rating). Without the channel field you can't compare channels later, and without an identifier you can't tell whether one angry customer wrote a review, filled in a survey and called twice.


Thematic connects to survey tools such as Qualtrics and Medallia, support tools such as Zendesk and Salesforce, and review sources such as Trustpilot, the App Store and Google Play. Call transcripts usually come in through the API, a data warehouse such as Snowflake or BigQuery, or a file upload, because most call recording platforms export text rather than connect directly.


The plumbing itself (connectors, schema, deduplication) is covered in our guide to[creating a single source of truth for customer feedback](https://getthematic.com/insights/single-source-of-truth-customer-feedback) . This article picks up once the data is in one place.


## Step 2: Prepare call transcripts before you analyze them


A transcript is not a survey comment, and[contact center conversations](https://getthematic.com/insights/contact-center-conversations-insights) need their own preparation. A ten-minute call contains the agent's script, hold messages, identity checks and the customer's actual problem, often in that order. If you analyze the whole thing, themes like "verification" and "greeting" will look like your biggest issues.


Three preparation rules make transcripts comparable with shorter feedback:


- **Analyze the customer's turns, not the agent's.** The agent's script repeats on every call and drowns out what the customer said.
- **Separate the contact reason from the root cause.** "Calling about a declined payment" is the reason. "The app didn't explain why it was declined" is the cause, and the cause is what other channels will mention.
- **Remove bot and interactive voice response (IVR) turns** before the text reaches your analysis.


This matters because most contact centers only ever look at a sliver of calls.[ISG Research](https://research.isg-one.com/viewpoints/customer_experience/contact-center-quality-processes-must-modernize-for-the-digital-era) found that the share of interactions typically scored for quality is "as little as 1% to 3% of the total." Analyzing every transcript changes what you can see, but only if the text you analyze is the customer's.


## Step 3: Code every channel against one theme set


This is the step most programs skip. The survey platform has its own categories, the review tool has its own tags, and the contact center has disposition codes. Three taxonomies mean three answers to "what's our biggest problem?", and no way to add them up.


One theme set fixes that. "Delivery delays" in a survey, "where is my order" on a call and "parcel never arrived" in a review should all land in the same theme. Thematic's lenses do this directly. A lens combines one or more datasets and analyzes them with a single, unified set of themes, and when you add a new data source to an existing lens, it automatically picks up the lens's themes. Thematic builds a two-level taxonomy of themes and subthemes from the comments themselves, so channel-specific wording still maps to a shared parent theme.


Regulators work the same way. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)[received more than 6.6 million complaints in 2025](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_2025-cr-annual-report_2026-03.pdf) and analyzes the narrative text consumers provide, rather than relying on the category a company picked. ISO 10002, the International Organization for Standardization's standard for complaints handling, includes analyzing and evaluating complaints to improve products and services.


## Step 4: Compare each theme's share within each channel


Once every channel shares a theme set, the temptation is to add up mentions across channels. Don't. Each channel has its own bias:


- **Surveys** reach only the customers you chose to ask and who chose to answer.
- **[Reviews](https://getthematic.com/insights/review-analysis)** are public and skew toward the extremes.
- **Calls** come from customers who couldn't fix the problem themselves, so they skew negative.


[Qualtrics found](https://www.qualtrics.com/articles/news/increased-expectations-declining-loyalty-qualtrics-announces-2025-consumer-experience-trends/) that less than a third of consumers give feedback directly to a company, and that consumers are 8 points less likely to say anything after a bad experience than in 2021.[Gartner also found](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-07-23-gartner-survey-finds-more-than-half-of-customer-service-journeys-now-start-on-third-party-platforms) that 51% of service journeys now begin on third-party platforms, and only 22% of customers start, stay and resolve their issue entirely in a company's own channels. Each channel shows you a different slice of customers.


So compare shares within each channel. A theme in 4% of survey comments, 6% of reviews and 18% of calls is an operational issue: customers can't fix it themselves. A theme strong in reviews but absent from calls is often a brand or product perception problem.


Volume is the other trap. A contact center with 50,000 transcripts will outweigh a survey with 500 comments in any combined total. Thematic's lenses handle both problems. You can place datasets side by side for comparison, and dataset weighting lets you decide how much influence each dataset has, no matter how big or small it is. With weighting on, each dataset's theme percentage is worked out inside that dataset first, then blended by the ratios you set.


## Step 5: Rank issues by impact and cost


Frequency tells you what's loud, not what matters, which is why[the most common complaints aren't always the biggest problems](https://getthematic.com/insights/most-common-complaints-arent-biggest-problems) . A theme mentioned by thousands of mildly annoyed customers can matter less than one mentioned by a few hundred who are about to leave.


Rank on two measures instead:


- **Score impact.** Thematic's impact score shows how much your overall score would change if you removed every comment mentioning a theme, so it weighs how badly a theme scores against how many people raise it. See[how to find what's driving your NPS](https://getthematic.com/insights/find-what-is-driving-nps-score) .
- **Cost.** Count the contacts each theme generates in the call channel. A theme that drives calls is costing money every day it isn't fixed. On lenses, Thematic's[Revenue at Risk](https://getthematic.com/insights/revenue-at-risk-customer-feedback) puts an estimated dollar value on every theme.


A theme that ranks high on both, and shows up in more than one channel, goes to the top of the list. Then open the comments behind it in each channel. That's where the fix becomes obvious.


## A worked example: a UK digital bank


Atom Bank, a UK financial services company, brought seven channels together in Thematic, including in-product feedback, reviews, complaints, call-center notes and customer relationship management (CRM) data. It reported them on one 1-to-100 Customer Goodwill Score across three product lines.


Atom Bank reports 69% fewer calls about unaccepted mortgage requests. Michael Sherwood, Head of CX at Atom Bank, described the wider effect: "With the insights, we've seen significant improvements, such as a 30% decrease in contact centre failure."


The point for contact center leaders: call volume is where an issue shows up, not always where it starts. Putting call-center notes in the same view as reviews, complaints and in-product feedback is what lets a team find the cause behind a contact reason, rather than just counting the calls.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Keeping one taxonomy per tool.** You can't add up three sets of categories. Code everything against one theme set.
- **Analyzing the whole transcript.** Agent scripts and verification steps become your biggest "issues." Analyze the customer's words.
- **Adding counts across channels.** Channels have different biases. Compare shares within each channel.
- **Ranking by volume.** Rank by score impact and contact cost instead.
- **Sampling calls.** Scoring 1% to 3% of calls hides the issues that matter. Analyze all of them.
- **Stopping at the theme.** Read the comments behind the top theme in each channel before you decide on a fix.


## The short answer


To find customer issues across surveys, reviews and call center transcripts, bring every channel in with a date, channel and customer ID, strip call transcripts down to the customer's words, code everything against one theme set, compare each theme's share within each channel, and rank by impact and contact cost. Thematic's lenses analyze every channel with one set of themes, so the same issue has the same name everywhere. Start with the theme that shows up in both your calls and your reviews.
